what: Choice Hotels franchises hotel brands. It licenses names including Comfort Inn, Quality Inn, Sleep Inn, Econo Lodge, Cambria and Radisson to independent hotel owners, who pay a percentage of room revenue in exchange for the brand, the booking system and the loyalty programme.
customers: Hotel owners, mostly small operators of economy, midscale and upscale properties across the United States and internationally, and the travellers who book through Choice’s brands.
money: A percentage of room revenue from about 7,500 franchised hotels.
Fees collected from franchisees to fund marketing and booking systems, largely passed through.
A small number of owned properties and other services.
moat: Franchising requires almost no capital: Choice collects a share of room revenue without owning hotels, employing staff or paying for renovations. Its brands are well established in the economy and midscale segments where an independent owner most needs a recognised name and a booking channel, and the loyalty programme delivers bookings an independent could not generate.
risks: Seventeen analysts average a $117.18 target, below the current price of $120.05 — an unusual signal that the sell side sees the shares as fully valued.
Revenue has flattened at about $1.6B, so room revenue across the franchised system is not growing.
Debt of $2.0B against $45.0M of cash is substantial for a company of this size.
The shares trade at about 26.6 times earnings and 17.0 times EV/EBITDA, a full price for a business without growth.
Franchisees are small operators who struggle to fund renovations, and tired properties damage the brand Choice licenses.
opportunities: The franchise model requires almost no capital, which is why a 23.2% net margin is possible on a hotel business.
Revenue grew from $1.1B in 2021 to $1.6B, and royalty revenue is contractual rather than operational.
Economy and midscale travellers are less discretionary than luxury guests, which makes the segment steadier in a downturn.
The Radisson acquisition added upscale brands and international reach at little incremental cost.
Loyalty programme members book directly, which reduces the commission paid to online travel agents.
watch: Net room growth and revenue per available room across the system. A franchisor earns a percentage of someone else’s revenue, so hotel count and room rates are the only two levers it has.
view: Hotel franchising is a far better business than hotel owning, and the margin tells you why: Choice earns a 23.2% net margin on a hotel business, which is impossible if you actually own hotels. It collects a percentage of room revenue from about 7,500 properties while owning almost none of them, employing almost none of the staff, and paying for none of the renovations. The asset is the brand and the booking system.

The segment it serves is the right one for franchising. An independent owner of a midscale roadside hotel cannot generate bookings or trust alone, so the brand above the door and the loyalty programme behind it are worth paying for. A luxury hotel can largely attract guests on its own, which is why franchising matters less at the top end. Choice’s brands — Comfort Inn, Quality Inn, Sleep Inn — are unglamorous and precisely positioned.

The weakness is structural to the model and shows in the numbers. Revenue has flattened at about $1.6 billion, which for a franchisor means room revenue across the system is not growing. The franchisees are small operators who find it hard to finance the renovations the brand requires, and a tired property both earns less and damages the name. Choice’s leverage to force upgrades is limited, because the owner can always defect to a rival brand.

At 26.6 times earnings and 17 times EV/EBITDA, with $2.0 billion of debt against $45 million of cash and seventeen analysts averaging a target below the share price, the market is paying a quality multiple for a no-growth franchise with real leverage. The model deserves a premium; this particular price assumes a recovery in system room revenue that the recent figures do not support. Net room growth and revenue per available room are the two numbers, and both need to turn before the multiple makes sense.
bull: Room revenue recovers across the system, Radisson adds international and upscale rooms at little cost, and a capital-free 23% margin model compounds.
bear: Franchisees defer renovations and system room revenue keeps stagnating, while $2.0 billion of debt sits beneath a 27 times earnings multiple on no growth.
